feedback.pattern: Return value logic error in remove method
feedback.explanation: This test regressed immediately after the initial remove implementation at run 45, failing because the remove method was not returning the correct value (the removed node or its replacement). The error persisted through runs 45–50 despite multiple code adjustments. At run 51, a 5-line removal and 1-line addition to BinarySearchTree.java changed the return value logic. The test then passed consistently. The semantic context shows multiple remove-related tests were being debugged simultaneously. The fix at run 51 specifically modified how the method communicates the removed or promoted node back to the caller, which is essential for maintaining tree structure integrity when the caller needs to update parent pointers or verify the operation.
nextSteps: Review the contract of your remove method: it should return the node that replaces the removed node's position in the tree (either a child, a successor, or null). Ensure every code path—leaf removal, single-child removal, and two-child removal—returns the correct replacement node, not the removed node itself.

Trace through a two-child removal scenario on paper: when removing a node with two children, you promote the in-order successor (or predecessor) to replace it. Verify that your return statement reflects the promoted node, not the original removed node, so the parent can correctly update its child pointer.

Test your return logic by writing a small helper method that validates the tree structure after each remove operation—check that parent pointers are consistent and that the tree remains a valid BST. This will catch return value errors that cause structural corruption.

feedback.pattern: Infinite recursion and tree structure corruption in remove method
feedback.explanation: This test failed immediately at run 45 when remove was first implemented, then triggered compilation or execution errors at runs 47–48 (likely infinite recursion or null pointer dereference). The test remained failing through run 49. A 5-line removal and 1-line addition at run 50 resolved the issue. The semantic context indicates multiple remove-related tests were being debugged simultaneously. The fix at run 50 modified the recursive logic or base case handling. Subsequent code changes at runs 54–55 (14 lines removed, 3 added; then 19 lines removed and 19 added) further refined the implementation, but the fundamental fix came at run 50 when the infinite recursion or structural corruption was eliminated.
nextSteps: Examine your remove method's base cases and recursive calls carefully: ensure that each recursive call operates on a strictly smaller subtree (left or right child), and that you have a clear termination condition (e.g., when the node to remove is found or when you reach a null). Infinite recursion often occurs when the recursive call doesn't make progress toward the base case.

For the two-child case, verify that after promoting the in-order successor (or predecessor), you recursively remove that successor from its original location in the right (or left) subtree. The recursive call must be on the correct child and must update the node's child pointer with the result of the recursive call.

Add assertions or debug output to trace the recursion depth and node values during removal of a node with two children. This will help you spot if the recursion is revisiting the same node or failing to update parent pointers correctly.

feedback.pattern: Iterator initialization and traversal logic error
feedback.explanation: This test took 14 runs to resolve, spanning from run 26 to run 40. The error evolved from an initial NullPointerException in iterator initialization (run 26) to an assertion error expecting 2 but receiving 1 (run 27), then to a null return value (run 29). A regression occurred at run 28 affecting 10 tests, but the test recovered at run 29. The test remained failing through run 39 despite no visible code changes in the semantic context between runs 30 and 40. At run 40, a significant code change (3 lines removed, 13 lines added) resolved the issue. The 13-line addition at run 40 modified the traversal mechanism—either the initialization of the traversal stack or queue, or the logic for advancing to the next node.
nextSteps: Ensure your iterator correctly initializes its traversal state before the first call to next(). For an in-order traversal, this typically means pushing all left-child nodes onto a stack starting from the root. Verify that hasNext() correctly reflects whether there are unvisited nodes remaining, and that next() advances the iterator state before returning the current node's value.

Implement a clear traversal algorithm on paper first: decide whether you're doing in-order, pre-order, or level-order traversal, and trace through a small tree (e.g., 3 nodes) to ensure your stack or queue operations are correct. Common mistakes include forgetting to push children after visiting a node, or returning the wrong node value.

Test your iterator in isolation: create a simple tree, iterate through it, and verify the order of values matches your intended traversal. Use a separate method to print the tree in the same order and compare the outputs.

feedback.pattern: Logic error in non-BST search implementation
feedback.explanation: This test failed for 8 runs starting from run 1 (initial implementation) through run 8, with the error consistently being an assertion failure (expected true, got false). The containsNonBST() method was implemented at run 3, which compiled but had incorrect logic. Runs 4–8 showed no code changes and no test result changes. At run 9, a 20-line addition to BinarySearchTree.java resolved the issue. The semantic context shows multiple methods were being implemented in early runs (isEmpty at run 2, containsNonBST at run 3). The containsNonBST method requires a search strategy that examines both left and right subtrees regardless of the comparison result, since the tree is not guaranteed to be a valid BST.
nextSteps: Understand the key difference between contains() and containsNonBST(): the former can eliminate half the tree based on BST ordering, but the latter must search both subtrees because the tree structure may not respect BST properties. Write containsNonBST() as a full tree search: check the current node, then recursively search both left and right children, returning true if the value is found in any subtree.

Use a logical OR to combine results from both subtrees: return (current node matches) OR (found in left subtree) OR (found in right subtree). Ensure you don't short-circuit the search prematurely—both subtrees must be checked even if the current node matches.

Test containsNonBST() on a deliberately unbalanced or invalid tree (e.g., a tree where the right child of a node is smaller than the node). Verify it finds values that a BST-based search would miss due to incorrect tree structure.

feedback.pattern: Complex removal case handling (two-child nodes) with tree structure corruption
feedback.explanation: This test took 10 attempts across 7 failed runs (runs 45–55) to resolve. It failed immediately at run 45 when remove was first implemented, then experienced a compilation or execution error at runs 47–48 and again at run 52. The semantic context shows that by run 51, simpler remove tests (testRemove and testRemoveReturnValue) had been fixed, but testRemoveAdvanced remained failing with an assertion error. At run 55, a substantial refactor (19 lines removed, 19 lines added) resolved the issue. The pattern indicates the code changes were focused on advanced removal scenarios—likely the two-child case where an in-order successor or predecessor must be promoted, including successor/predecessor selection, recursive removal of the successor, or tree restructuring after promotion.
nextSteps: Implement the two-child removal case step-by-step: (1) find the in-order successor (leftmost node in the right subtree) or predecessor (rightmost node in the left subtree), (2) copy its value to the node being removed, (3) recursively remove the successor/predecessor from its original location, and (4) update the node's right (or left) child pointer with the result of the recursive call. Verify each step independently.

Trace through a concrete example on paper: remove a node with two children from a tree with at least 5 nodes. Draw the tree before and after, showing which node is promoted and how parent pointers are updated. Ensure the final tree is still a valid BST.

Add a validation method that checks BST properties after each remove: for every node, all values in the left subtree are smaller and all values in the right subtree are larger. Run this after each test case to catch structural corruption early.
